documento.autoria: Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC)

resumen_enriquecido.pregunta_investigacion: How can Caribbean small island developing States (SIDS) transition from vulnerability to resilience and sustainable development with equality, given their structural economic, social, and environmental constraints and the intensifying impacts of climate change?

alcance.referentes_dependencias: Latin America, OECD countries, European Union, Republic of Korea, United States
alcance.sectorial: Multisectoral (Economics, Trade, Social Protection, Education, Health, Energy, Environment)

hallazgos_principales: Caribbean economies have experienced persistent low growth, averaging 0.8% annually since 2010, significantly lagging behind other small States (4.7%) (p. 23).
Public debt in the subregion remains among the highest in the world, with two-thirds of CARICOM countries exceeding the 60% debt-to-GDP sustainability threshold in 2016 (p. 26).
The Caribbean share of global merchandise trade fell by a third from 0.14% in 1990 to 0.092% in 2016, reflecting declining export competitiveness (p. 25).
Average annual loss from hurricanes is estimated at US$ 835 million, with individual disasters costing between 33% and 200% of a country's GDP (p. 27, 29).
Youth unemployment is among the highest in the world, averaging nearly 25%, with young women reaching rates over 30% (p. 63).
The subregion is the global epicenter of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), which account for 70% of all deaths (p. 77).

conclusiones: The Caribbean's transition to resilience is hindered by entrenched structural imbalances in trade and fiscal accounts, exacerbated by frequent natural disasters (p. 24, 27).
Sustainable development with equality requires a paradigm shift from a cost-based narrative to one of opportunities in sectors like the blue economy and creative industries (p. 44, 46).
Institutional capacity and data generation are critical bottlenecks that prevent the effective implementation and monitoring of the SDGs and the SAMOA Pathway (p. 19, 99).
recomendaciones: Implement the ECLAC Debt for Climate Adaptation Swap Initiative to create fiscal space and establish a Caribbean Resilience Fund (CRF) for green investment (p. 31, 101).
Deepen regional integration via the CARICOM Single Market and Economy (CSME) and create a Single ICT Space to overcome lack of economies of scale (p. 14, 102).
Reform the education system through the CARICOM Human Resource Development 2030 Strategy, focusing on STEM and competency-based training (p. 36, 103).
Transition to sustainable energy matrices by increasing the share of renewables and improving energy efficiency in transportation and infrastructure (p. 37, 107).
Mainstream a gender perspective across all national development plans and implement time-use surveys to quantify and address unpaid care work (p. 17, 104).

resumen_enriquecido.resumen_narrativo: This 2018 Outlook provides a comprehensive analysis of the development challenges and opportunities facing the Caribbean subregion. It identifies a 'silent crisis' of unsustainable debt and low growth, exacerbated by the increasing frequency of category five hurricanes. The document proposes a strategic 'Caribbean first' approach, centered on the innovative Debt for Climate Adaptation Swap Initiative to unleash financing for resilience. It argues for structural transformation through the blue economy and creative industries, while emphasizing the need for a seamless education system and robust social protection floors to achieve sustainable development with equality by 2030.

resumen_secciones.seccion: I. From vulnerability to resilience: creating the Caribbean future we want
resumen_secciones.resumen: Sets the conceptual framework by defining Caribbean SIDS as a 'special case' for sustainable development. It argues that the subregion's development trajectory is increasingly uncertain due to low growth and climate change. It outlines the necessity of mainstreaming global agendas into national development plans, supported by regional integration and multi-stakeholder partnerships. It identifies gender equality, ICT for development, and robust statistics as critical cross-cutting keys for implementation.

dimensiones.cita: specifically declared that small island developing States (SIDS) “are a special case both for environment and development” support.
The strategy being pursued in the subregion is the embedding, or mainstreaming, of these interrelated global frameworks

subsecciones.resumen: Provides context on the emergence of the SIDS category in the international arena, tracing the recognition of their unique challenges from the Earth Summit in 1992 to the adoption of the SAMOA Pathway. It frames the Caribbean's quest for sustainable development as an ongoing challenge of overcoming inherent structural disadvantages, such as small landmass and limited resource bases, which require specialized global support frameworks.

Identifies the core obstacles to progress, specifically focusing on the 'silent crisis' of unsustainable debt and the sharp erosion of merchandise trade competitiveness over the last three decades. It highlights the devastating economic impact of natural disasters, which can wipe out years of development gains in a single event. Social stressors like high youth unemployment and the brain drain of tertiary-educated individuals are also examined as barriers to long-term stability.

Proposes a holistic approach to building subregional resilience. This comprehensive subsection covers the mainstreaming of the 2030 Agenda and the SAMOA Pathway into national strategies, the vital role of regional integration through CARICOM and the OECS, and the critical cross-cutting keys: achieving gender equality, leveraging ICT for developmental gains, and generating high-quality disaggregated data. It emphasizes that achieving the SDGs in the Caribbean requires a 'Caribbean first' strategy and the institutionalization of evidence-based policy processes. Furthermore, it highlights that the successful implementation of these frameworks will depend on strong multi-stakeholder involvement, increased public awareness, and sustained political buy-in across the subregion to ensure that policies remain consistent over time and across different sectors.

Summarizes the chapter's key messages, reiterating that the Caribbean subregion stands at a critical juncture where only integrated and coordinated action across economic, social, and environmental pillars can secure a sustainable future. It calls for a paradigm shift from reactive crisis management to proactive, long-term strategic planning and regional cooperation to overcome the limitations of scale and build lasting resilience.

resumen_secciones.seccion: II. The Caribbean economy: from constraints to opportunities
resumen_secciones.resumen: Analyzes the economic structural imbalances, specifically current account deficits and the unsustainable debt crisis, exacerbated by de-risking and threats to offshore financial centers. It proposes an industrial strategy based on structural transformation and competitiveness enhancers such as skills development, sustainable energy, and infrastructure. The chapter highlights three strategic pillars for repositioning the subregion: integration into regional value chains, development of the blue economy, and strengthening creative industries to generate high value-added employment.

subsecciones.resumen: Documents the persistent low growth of Caribbean economies, which have averaged only 0.8% annually since 2010, significantly lagging behind other small States. It links this chronic underperformance to the subregion's inability to participate effectively in the expansion of global trade and its continued reliance on a narrow range of service exports, making it highly vulnerable to external volatility.

Details the interconnected debt crisis and persistent trade deficits. It discusses how frequent and intensifying hurricanes undermine fiscal stability, forcing governments into a cycle of borrowing for reconstruction. The section also examines the negative effects of 'de-risking' by global banks on financial inclusion and offshore financial centers. It strongly advocates for the ECLAC Debt for Climate Adaptation Swap as a transformative mechanism to convert debt service into resilience investments, noting that high financing costs and primary deficits further fuel this 'silent crisis' of debt that currently affects 11 of 13 Caribbean small States.

dimensiones.cita: In 2016, two thirds of the CARICOM member countries had debt-to-GDP ratios above the 60% threshold
The Caribbean subregion fell behind other developing countries, and the global economy, both in its goods and services exports

subsecciones.resumen: Identifies the 'middle-income trap' and argues for an industrial policy focused on enabling factors like skills development, sustainable energy transition, and modernized physical and digital infrastructure. It highlights the high cost of electricity (often 3x higher than in the USA) and the educational mismatch as major drags on productivity, proposing the use of blended financing and public-private partnerships (PPPs) to bridge the infrastructure and energy gaps. In this regard, it mentions the Regional PPP Support Facility established by the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), and the Caribbean Development Bank (CDB) to build capacity and support the development of viable projects in the subregion.

dimensiones.cita: The Caribbean economy will remain in the middle-income trap where it has been for several years
Innovative financing instruments, such as combining loans and grants in blended financing, is an option to address

subsecciones.seccion: D. Value chains, E. Blue economy and F. Creative industries
subsecciones.resumen: Explores new growth frontiers for the subregion. It frames the Caribbean as 'large ocean States' that must leverage their extensive exclusive economic zones for sustainable marine biotechnology and fisheries. It also identifies cultural and creative industries (music, animation, design) as high-growth sectors with strong potential for generating quality employment for youth and women, provided there is a supportive intellectual property and financing framework.

dimensiones.cita: Small island States have been described as large ocean States because the oceans and seas

subsecciones.resumen: Recaps the economic agenda, emphasizing that overcoming structural constraints requires a decisive shift towards innovation-led growth, regional coordination in industrial policy, and the adoption of modern financing instruments to unleash the potential of new sectors like the blue and creative economies for sustainable prosperity.

resumen_secciones.seccion: III. Social development: a path to empowerment and inclusion
resumen_secciones.resumen: Addresses the erosion of human development gains due to social spending contraction and debt servicing. It focuses on multidimensional poverty, women's empowerment, and human capital development. The chapter critiques the 'failing' education system and highlights the demographic shift and the epidemic of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) as primary threats to productivity and inclusion.

subsecciones.seccion: A. Addressing poverty, social exclusion and inequalities
subsecciones.resumen: Analyzes the stagnation in poverty reduction across the Caribbean and the rise of income inequality. It emphasizes that despite high GDP per capita in some nations, multidimensional poverty remains high because of the subregion's extreme vulnerability to economic and environmental shocks, which can quickly push vulnerable households back into poverty levels.

dimensiones.cita: In the Caribbean, the country poverty assessments (CPAs) conducted regularly by the Caribbean Development Bank have shown, despite data gaps, that high proportions of Caribbean populations live below the poverty line (see table 5).

subsecciones.seccion: B. Advancing women’s empowerment and autonomy
subsecciones.resumen: Discusses the persistent barriers to gender equality, including the vastly unequal distribution of unpaid care work and lower labor market participation rates for women despite their higher average education levels. It calls for the mandatory mainstreaming of gender in all national development plans and the implementation of time-use surveys to inform effective policy making.

subsecciones.seccion: C. Human capital development, education and capacity-building
subsecciones.resumen: Critiques the obsolete education model and the 'leaking' pipeline where only 15% of students reach tertiary education, with significant failure rates in literacy and mathematics. It advocates for the CARICOM Human Resource Development 2030 Strategy to create a competency-based training (CBET) and life-long learning system that addresses the requirements of the fourth industrial revolution. It also proposes the use of disruptive technologies like blockchain for secure and portable qualifications management. Furthermore, the section addresses the severe brain drain affecting the subregion, noting that emigration rates for tertiary-educated individuals are among the highest in the world, reaching as much as 93% in Guyana and 89% in Suriname, which severely depletes the subregion's intellectual and productive capital.

dimensiones.cita: the Caribbean education system, of which certifying and examinations bodies

subsecciones.seccion: D. Two age groups in focus: youth and older persons
subsecciones.resumen: Examines the dual challenges of exceptionally high youth unemployment (averaging 25%) and the emerging health and care needs of an ageing population. It proposes strengthening intergenerational ties and modernizing social services to ensure that both age groups can contribute to and benefit from a more inclusive development path for the subregion.

subsecciones.seccion: E. Social protection: catalyst for sustainable development
subsecciones.resumen: Argues for the establishment of robust social protection floors that are specifically designed to be resilient to the frequent natural disasters of the subregion. It emphasizes that social protection should be viewed as a critical investment in human capital and risk management rather than a mere fiscal burden on state budgets.

subsecciones.seccion: F. Non-communicable diseases (NCDs) in the Caribbean
subsecciones.resumen: Reports that the Caribbean has become the global epicenter of NCDs, which now account for 70% of all deaths in the subregion. It details the massive economic burden these diseases place on productivity and health systems, calling for the urgent implementation of the Port of Spain Declaration and Agenda 2030 health targets for NCD reduction.

dimensiones.cita: The subregion is the global epicentre of NCDs, with 70% of all deaths attributable to these diseases

subsecciones.resumen: Consolidates the social policy recommendations of the chapter, focusing on a multi-pronged approach to empowerment, social inclusion, and the protection of the most vulnerable groups through evidence-based interventions and strengthened regional health and education frameworks for a resilient social fabric.

resumen_secciones.seccion: IV. Environmental management: vulnerability, constraints and opportunities
resumen_secciones.resumen: Examines the environmental pillar of resilience, focusing on climate change adaptation, disaster risk management (DRM), and water security. It highlights the exposure of coastal settlements and the need for energy transition in isolated power systems. It advocates for proactive DRM integrated into public investment systems.

subsecciones.resumen: Describes the Caribbean's extreme hazard vulnerability as the second most disaster-prone region globally. It identifies the 2017 hurricane season as a tipping point for the subregion and emphasizes the urgent need for resilient infrastructure, settlement relocation strategies, and the protection of marine biodiversity as natural buffers. In this context, it notes that ECLAC led Damage and Loss Assessments (DaLA) in five of the countries affected by Irma and Maria —Anguilla, the Bahamas, British Virgin Islands, Sint Maarten, and Turks and Caicos Islands— highlighting the massive scale of the impacts.

dimensiones.cita: The Caribbean is the second most hazard-prone region in the world, due to both its geographical location
ECLAC led damage and loss assessments in five of the countries affected by the two most powerful storm systems

subsecciones.seccion: B. Water resources and solid waste management
subsecciones.resumen: Analyzes the growing water scarcity challenges caused by climate-induced drying and the systemic inefficiencies in solid waste management. It proposes the adoption of integrated water resources management (IWRM) and circular economy approaches to waste to enhance environmental health and resource efficiency.

dimensiones.cita: Although there is an increasing trend to mainstream water resources management at the local and regional level, countries in the subregion have yet to implement adequate governance frameworks to fully support their initiatives.

subsecciones.seccion: C. Energy transition and D. Sustainable transportation
subsecciones.resumen: Analyzes the vast potential for renewable energy development and provides a roadmap for the electrification of government fleets as a pilot for wider transition. It emphasizes that modernized energy matrices significantly reduce external economic vulnerability and enhance the resilience of critical infrastructure during disasters.

dimensiones.cita: Caribbean countries can develop or access almost all renewable energy technologies known today

subsecciones.resumen: Summarizes the environmental agenda, stressing that environmental sustainability and effective disaster risk management are the non-negotiable foundation upon which all other pillars of development in Caribbean SIDS must be built to ensure long-term survival and prosperity in a changing climate.

resumen_secciones.seccion: V. A way forward: policy considerations and recommendations
resumen_secciones.resumen: Synthesizes the policy agenda across global alignment, cross-cutting issues, partnerships, economic transformation, social development, and environmental sustainability. It prioritizes the Debt for Climate Adaptation Swap and the Caribbean Resilience Fund as the primary engines for financing resilience and structural change.

dimensiones.cita: Caribbean partners, and the wider global community, should be encouraged to strongly support the ECLAC Debt

subsecciones.resumen: Provides specific recommendations on mainstreaming the SDGs into national planning processes and resisting the 'graduation' of Caribbean SIDS based purely on GDP per capita criteria, which ignores their extreme vulnerability and lack of access to concessional financing.

dimensiones.cita: Every Caribbean country should prioritize drawing up an integrated, long-term national development plan.

subsecciones.resumen: Outlines concrete action items on achieving gender equality through national plans, utilizing ICTs for regional development, and building the necessary statistical capacities to generate the disaggregated data required for evidence-based decision-making and monitoring.

Focuses on the importance of south-south and triangular cooperation to leverage regional expertise and resources. It calls for strengthened partnerships between Caribbean countries and the wider international community to support the subregion's resilience goals.

Sets out normative steps for implementing the ECLAC Debt Swap Initiative and the creation of the Caribbean Resilience Fund. It also advocates for deepening the CSME and implementing industrial policies that target new growth frontiers in the blue and creative economies.

Consolidates recommendations for radical education reform, the reduction of NCD prevalence through regional health cooperation, and the establishment of comprehensive, disaster-resilient social protection floors to empower and include all Caribbean citizens.

Identifies urgent actions for proactive disaster risk management, the transition to sustainable energy Matrices, and water security. It emphasizes the integration of environmental considerations into all aspects of national public investment and development planning.

dimensiones.cita: Governments and stakeholders should step up efforts and enforce measures to protect ecosystems and the services they provide.

gran_impulso_ambiental_concreto.evidencia: El documento propone un paquete coordinado de inversiones y cambios de política, específicamente a través de la 'Iniciativa de Canje de Deuda por Adaptación al Clima' y la creación de un 'Fondo de Resiliencia del Caribe' (p. 31, 101). Se enfoca en sectores estratégicos como la energía renovable (p. 37), la economía azul (p. 44) y las industrias creativas (p. 46), conectándolos con las 'tres eficiencias' (innovación schumpeteriana, empleo keynesiano y desacoplamiento ambiental) (p. 45, 47).

citas.cita: is based on the creation of a Caribbean Resilience Fund (CRF) which is expected to provide financing

articulacion_actores.evidencia: El informe identifica varios mecanismos regionales específicos de coordinación, como la Agencia de Salud Pública del Caribe (CARPHA) (p. 76), el Centro de Cambio Climático de la Comunidad del Caribe (CCCCC) (p. 82), la Agencia del Caribe para el Manejo de Emergencias en Desastres (CDEMA) (p. 105) y la Iniciativa del Desafío del Caribe (CCI) (p. 48). Estas son plataformas institucionalizadas para la colaboración entre múltiples países y actores dentro de la subregión.

citas.cita: the Caribbean Challenge Initiative (CCI). This was launched initially in 2008 and brings together a number of Caribbean States and territories, the private sector, and other partners —governments, funding agencies and NGOs— in an endeavour aimed at conserving and sustainably managing the subregion’s marine and coastal environment.

oportunidades_productivas_sostenibles.evidencia: El documento enumera sectores sostenibles específicos como la economía azul (biotecnología marina, turismo sostenible) y las industrias creativas (audiovisuales, medios interactivos) y desarrolla explícitamente su vínculo con el empleo y la productividad, especialmente para jóvenes y mujeres (p. 45, 47). También identifica las 'industrias verdes' como un nicho para el crecimiento futuro (p. 96).

citas.cita: the global reach of the cultural and creative industries (design, music, arts, audiovisuals, film-making, publishing, animation)

como_hacerlo_concreto.evidencia: The final chapter 'A way forward' (p. 99-108) contains a detailed list of normative recommendations. Of the 43 items analyzed across six subsections, the majority (34) are concrete, naming specific instruments (Debt Swap, CRF, CSME), delivered products (time-use surveys, building codes, national development plans), or responsible entities.

citas.cita: Every Caribbean country should prioritize drawing up an integrated, long-term national development plan.

desglose_items.item: Institutionalize evidence-based processes and formalize national statistical systems
Draft, review and adopt national gender equality policies and plans
Implement the ECLAC Debt for Climate Adaptation Swap Initiative and create the CRF
Promote free movement of goods, people, services, capital and technology under CSME
Regulate access and downstream use of marine genetic resources in EEZs under Nagoya Protocol
Apply blockchain technology for qualifications management and digital certifications
Carry out time-use surveys to assess disproportionate responsibilities of women
Establish a social protection floor and promote non-contributory pension schemes
Adopt grid hardening strategies including underground networks and eliminating system redundancies
Include disaster risk management in the national public investment system

como_hacerlo_concreto.tally: 34 of 43 items pass the test of concrecion
como_hacerlo_concreto.nota: The tally covers all bulleted points in the summary sections A-F of Chapter V. Most items identify a specific instrument, delivered product or legislative reform.

razonamiento_5_pasos.tension_dialectica: The document addresses the contradiction between the Caribbean's middle-income status (which limits aid) and its extreme structural vulnerability (debt, disasters, small scale). It seeks to resolve this by shifting the region's focus from a cost-narrative of climate impact to an opportunity-narrative of resilience and economic transformation.
razonamiento_5_pasos.filtro_categoria_primaria: While the title is 'Outlook' and it covers economic and social issues, the core normative proposal is the 'Caribbean first' strategy and the institutional alignment required to manage resilience. It aims to transform state planning, regional integration, and financial governance (Capacidades del Estado) to handle environmental and economic shocks.
razonamiento_5_pasos.secundaria_obligatoria: Sostenibilidad ambiental is the secondary transformation because climate change and environmental management (blue economy, disaster risk reduction, energy transition) are the specific sector and restriction upon which the state capacities must be built and applied.
razonamiento_5_pasos.justificacion_anti_copia: The document focuses on the 'silent crisis' of debt, the proposed 'Debt for Climate Adaptation Swap', and the 'seamless' education reform. It frames the subregion as 'large ocean States' needing to leverage EEZs and blue biotechnology to escape the 'middle-income trap'.
razonamiento_5_pasos.validacion_anclas: Similar to Doc 10 (Agenda 2030) and Doc 19 (Management for climate action), it treats institutional architecture and planning as the primary object (#11) while environmental sustainability (#6) defines the scope and urgency of the action.
